about.title: about
about.content:
Hi, I’m Russell. I’m a Systems Administrator interested in infrastructure, automation, and homelabbing. Since I was young, I’ve been fascinated by automation - I fell in love with the idea that I could build a system once and have it handle repetitive work for me.
Growing up, online games helped develop that interest. Many of them involved complex systems that had to be understood and used efficiently, and I was especially drawn to mechanics that introduced automation or rewarded well-optimized workflows. I enjoyed learning how those systems worked, experimenting with different approaches, and finding ways to make the overall experience more efficient.
That curiosity eventually carried into my career. I’m naturally drawn to creating solutions that simplify work, reduce repetition, and improve consistency. At my current job, I use PowerShell to automate reporting, infrastructure tasks, and other processes that would otherwise require significant manual effort.
That same focus on practical automation has led me to incorporate agentic AI into my scripting workflow. I use it to prototype, refine, and troubleshoot scripts, which has helped me build several automations that reduce routine work and leave more time for higher-priority problems. AI helps me turn ideas into real implementations, while I remain responsible for carefully reviewing and testing the resulting code.
I also use agentic AI to support a personal knowledge workflow built around Obsidian. It gives me a context-aware way to organize, maintain, and build on my notes while I remain responsible for reviewing and approving the result.

Learn how to Automate Active Directory with Powershell. Follow along with this tutorial series to learn how you can automate your Users in Active Directory with PowerShell using a CSV files of employees. These short videos will teach you everything you need to know to make a fully functional automation script. Please like and subscribe.

18:30 · if you receive this awful purple screen just press Tab and enter now the system is updated you can check system processes like in Windows Task Manager with command top
18:45 · exit the top with simple keyboard combo control plus C that’s it you now have working proxmox virtualization server with one Ubuntu virtual machine you can see how much resources it uses under the virtual machine summary and the whole server usage under the server selection and summary we have come to the end of today’s video you can keep practicing by making more virtual machines testing some settings in them just play around and try not to break it till the next video haha if you

projects/aduseradmin.title: aduseradmin
projects/aduseradmin.content:
ADUserAdmin is a PowerShell and WPF application I created to make user provisioning more consistent in a hybrid Active Directory and Microsoft Entra environment. It grew from practical frustrations with the existing workflow and a desire to make the process easier for the team.
The tool has been used by eight teammates to provision at least 100 accounts. I estimate that it saves at least two minutes of direct entry time per account, but its more important benefit is the user experience: administrators can review and correct fields before submission instead of restarting the entire process after one incorrect value.
The problem
Our previous command-line workflow prompted for user details one field at a time. If an administrator entered an incorrect value, there was no practical way to return to that field; the process had to be restarted. Some attributes also had to be populated manually after account creation through Active Directory’s Attribute Editor.
I wanted to expose the full set of required onboarding fields in one interface, validate them before submission, and populate the account consistently in a single workflow. This reduced repetitive work while making it easier to compare the GUI against the onboarding request and catch mistakes before creating the account.
How it works

HR supplies an onboarding form containing the required account information, such as the employee identifier, email address, manager, department, and location.
An administrator selects the configured directory and enters the information into the GUI, where all fields can be reviewed and corrected.
The application validates the input, checks for conflicting accounts, resolves related values, and derives configured defaults.
PowerShell creates the Active Directory account with the specified attributes and places it in the organizational unit associated with the selected department.
The administrator starts an Entra Connect delta sync from the application so the new account can synchronize to Microsoft Entra ID.

The directory selector allows the same interface to route work through the appropriate configured domain or tenant without exposing environment-specific details in the public version.

Functionality
The public version demonstrates the main account-administration workflow:

search Active Directory and review account details in a user list;
create and edit users through guided forms;
populate names, email and sign-in values, title, department, manager, employee identifiers, contact information, and other organizational attributes;
derive location details and department-specific organizational-unit placement from reference data;
validate required fields and password complexity, detect conflicting account names, and resolve manager accounts;
generate secure passwords and manage account-enabled state;
record administrative activity through application logging; and
open a remote PowerShell session and trigger an Entra Connect delta sync.

The newer internal version also includes a field-normalization utility. An administrator can select a field such as department, find values that do not match the approved reference data, review the affected accounts, and normalize those values to the approved form. Logging has also been refined, including fixes that ensure updated employee fields are represented correctly.


Technologies

PowerShell implements orchestration, validation, user-management operations, logging, and remote commands.
WPF and XAML provide the desktop interface, with Material Design in XAML supplying the visual component library.
The Active Directory PowerShell module performs directory searches and account creation and updates.
Microsoft Graph PowerShell provides connectivity to Microsoft Entra, while PowerShell remoting connects to the synchronization server.
CSV reference data supplies approved departments and location-based defaults without hard-coding those values into the interface.
Visual Studio was used to design the original layout and work with the XAML.

Project structure
The sanitized public repository separates the interface, application state, and administrative operations into focused components:
ADUserAdmin/
├── start.ps1                         # Application launcher
├── ADUserAdminGUI.psm1               # Startup, orchestration, and event wiring
├── config/                           # Environment and application configuration
├── data/                             # Department and location reference data
├── resources/MainWindow.xaml         # WPF interface and Material Design layout
├── bin/                              # Material Design and XAML dependencies
└── modules/
    ├── ADUserAdminGUI.AppState/      # Shared configuration and UI state
    ├── ADUserAdminGUI.Logging/       # Activity and error logging
    ├── ADUserAdminGUI.PasswordUtil/  # Password generation and validation
    ├── ADUserAdminGUI.Sync/          # Remote session and delta-sync operations
    ├── ADUserAdminGUI.UI/            # UI initialization and navigation
    └── ADUserAdminGUI.UserManagement/ # AD search, creation, editing, and validation
Development approach
The GUI version took its name and initial functional direction from an earlier command-line tool created by our systems architect. I kept the familiar ADUserAdmin name because the new application served the same general workflow, but I wrote the GUI version from scratch in my own time. I independently reimplemented the required Entra Connect synchronization capability rather than copying the legacy code.
While building my version, I followed the Automate Active Directory with PowerShell tutorial series for its PowerShell and Active Directory foundation, then adapted and expanded the approach for our provisioning requirements. I completed the core functionality largely without AI assistance.
I initially laid out the WPF interface manually in Visual Studio and used Material Design in XAML to style it. As the interface grew, manually positioning every element became inefficient, so I later used AI to accelerate repetitive XAML generation while I continued to define the required behavior, connect the controls to PowerShell, and validate the resulting workflow.
Public repository context
The GitHub repository is a separate, organization-neutral edition I developed in my own time. The version used internally contains employer-specific configuration and newer functionality that are not included publicly. The public edition demonstrates the application’s structure and principal workflow without exposing employer branding, directory information, locations, reference data, or internal operational details.
What comes next
I am currently working with the same systems architect who created the original command-line tool on the design of a successor that would replace manual GUI entry with an export-driven workflow from the HR system. The goal is to compare approved employee data with directory accounts, update matching users, create missing users automatically, and eventually support offboarding. This work is still in progress and represents the next stage of the process automation rather than functionality in the public repository.

projects/homelab/background.title: background
projects/homelab/background.content:
Background and evolution
Starting with Proxmox
I started my homelab in May 2025 while we were migrating from ESXi to Proxmox at work. That experience inspired me to build my own Proxmox environment where I could experiment and become more familiar with the platform.
I was not ready to invest heavily in new hardware, so I wanted to see how much value I could get from a single ThinkPad T14. The constraint made the project more interesting: I could use Proxmox to build a virtualized environment and host several services on one machine. I followed a video guide to get the initial environment running.
Exploring self-hosting
After setting up Proxmox, I created a Docker virtual machine and began exploring self-hosted services. I experimented with Vaultwarden, Apache Guacamole, and Nginx Proxy Manager. Making a service available through my own domain was a small milestone, but it made the lab feel useful and motivated me to keep building. It also introduced me to the security and operational responsibility that comes with exposing a service beyond the local network.
Automation and development
I later created two additional virtual machines: an Ansible control node and a development environment. I used Ansible to experiment with repeatable system configuration and wrote a few playbooks for common setup tasks.
The development environment led me from Vim to Neovim and its large configuration ecosystem. I spent a great deal of time customizing it before realizing that the result had become difficult to organize and maintain. I restarted with a simpler setup based on LazyVim, which taught me that a smaller, dependable configuration is often more useful than endless customization.
What comes next
I am still running the lab on the original ThinkPad while I wait until I have room for future hardware upgrades. It now hosts several Compose projects and security controls alongside the original services. The lab continues to be a useful environment for self-directed learning and personal productivity.
I am learning Terraform for infrastructure provisioning, continuing to use Ansible for configuration, and planning to explore Kubernetes as the lab evolves.

projects/homelab/index.title: homelab
projects/homelab/index.content:
Homelab
My homelab is a small Proxmox environment that I use to explore virtualization, self-hosting, automation, security, and infrastructure as code. It began as a way to gain more experience with Proxmox and has grown into a practical place to run useful services and experiment outside of a production environment.
Overview
I started the lab in May 2025 on a single ThinkPad T14. Working within limited hardware has encouraged me to keep the environment deliberate and efficient while still giving me room to learn.

Background and evolution covers how the lab began and how my interests developed.
Current setup describes the environment, workloads, and direction of the lab.

Current architecture
Proxmox provides the virtualization layer for the lab. The current environment separates its responsibilities across four virtual machines:

an Ansible control node for automation;
a Docker host for persistent services and experiments;
a development workstation with browser-based and remote access; and
a small Windows virtual machine that is powered on only when needed.

Hosted services
Most applications run as Docker Compose projects on the Docker virtual machine.
Access and routing

Vaultwarden provides password management.
Apache Guacamole provides browser-based remote access.
Nginx Proxy Manager routes web traffic to the appropriate services.

Container maintenance

Watchtower checks for container-image updates.

Security

CrowdSec analyzes service logs and works with a firewall bouncer to block detected threats.

Automation and infrastructure as code
I use Ansible to experiment with repeatable system configuration. I am also learning Terraform with the goal of representing more of the lab as code, and I plan to use the environment to explore Kubernetes. The current Compose projects are stored in version control so their configuration is not tied only to the running Docker host.
Development environment
One virtual machine serves as a development environment. Experimenting with Vim, Neovim, and LazyVim taught me to prefer a simpler, maintainable configuration over endless customization.

projects/homelab/setup.title: setup
projects/homelab/setup.content:
Current setup
This page summarizes the documented environment without publishing internal addresses, port mappings, credentials, or storage paths.
Hardware
The lab currently runs on a Lenovo ThinkPad T14s Gen 2i with an Intel Core i5 processor, 8 GB of memory, internal NVMe storage, and external storage for backups and bulk data.
Virtualization
The machine runs a standalone Proxmox VE node. Proxmox lets me separate workloads into virtual machines while running the entire lab on one physical host.
Virtual machines






























RoleStatePurposeAnsible control nodeNormally runningAutomation experiments and repeatable Linux configurationDocker hostNormally runningCompose-based services and security toolingDevelopment workstationNormally runningLinux development, code-server, remote desktop, and isolated experimentationWindows utility VMOn demandWindows-specific testing and file-transfer tasks
Docker services
The Docker host runs several independently managed Compose projects.
Access and application delivery

Vaultwarden provides password management.
Apache Guacamole provides browser-based remote access.
Nginx Proxy Manager terminates and routes web traffic to internal services.

Container maintenance

Watchtower automates container-image update checks.

Security
CrowdSec analyzes authentication and reverse-proxy logs on the Docker host. Its firewall bouncer can block traffic associated with detected threats. This adds a security layer around the services that are reachable beyond the local network.
Automation
An Ansible control node is used to test playbooks and repeatable system configuration. I am learning Terraform so that infrastructure provisioning can become repeatable as well.
Development
A separate development virtual machine gives me a place to experiment with Linux tooling and editors without affecting the other workloads in the lab. It also gives me a persistent, fully personalized environment with my preferred tools and configuration available wherever I am.
I use NetBird as the VPN layer between my remote devices and the homelab. Once connected to my private NetBird network, I can reach the development VM and work in it over SSH without exposing the SSH service directly to the public internet.

projects/license-cost-recovery.title: license-cost-recovery
projects/license-cost-recovery.content:
Software License Cost Recovery Automation
This was an internal workplace project I implemented to centralize software-license assignments and turn them into department-level cost, budgeting, and optimization reports for services such as Microsoft 365, Zoom, and Adobe. It connects Microsoft Entra ID, PowerShell, Snipe-IT, MySQL, and Grafana.
The problem
Software access was assigned through Microsoft Entra ID groups, but calculating departmental costs required a consistent inventory of users, products, assignments, and pricing. Without a shared reporting layer, it was difficult to review who held each license, understand how software spending was distributed, or identify assignments that might be reclaimed or moved to a lower-cost tier.
The goal was to make the licensing data reviewable without treating the reporting system as the authority that grants or removes access.
How it works

LDAP synchronization maintains the user and department inventory in Snipe-IT.
A PowerShell workflow retrieves membership from Entra ID licensing groups.
The workflow maps those groups to Snipe-IT license records and updates assigned seats.
Snipe-IT stores the product, vendor, license tier, billing, cost, user, and department data used for reporting.
Grafana queries the Snipe-IT MySQL database and calculates assignment counts and monthly and annual costs.
Overview and department-level reports present the results for operational and budget review.

Reporting capabilities
The organization-level dashboard reports:

active license assignments and licensed users;
monthly and annual software costs;
costs grouped by software and department;
license distribution by product; and
per-user license and cost summaries.

The embedded Grafana reporting tool generates department-level output covering:

software breakdowns by vendor, tier, seat count, and cost;
detailed user-to-license assignments;
lower-cost tier comparisons;
reclaim and duplicate-assignment review;
overlapping-product review; and
fiscal-year budget and price-increase scenarios.

Technologies

PowerShell synchronizes Entra ID licensing-group membership with Snipe-IT license assignments.
Microsoft Entra ID remains the source of assigned software access.
Snipe-IT provides the centralized inventory of users, departments, software products, and assigned seats.
MySQL supplies the reporting data queried by Grafana.
Grafana provides the organization overview, department reports, budgeting calculations, optimization review, and embedded report generation.
LDAP maintains the underlying Snipe-IT user and department inventory.

projects/site.title: site
projects/site.content:
How the site works
Every post you see on this site is actually a .md file stored in my Obsidian vault. This is made possible with Quartz, which transforms the notes into a static website. My notes and the Quartz source are stored together in a private GitHub repo, while the generated website is published to a separate public repo through GitHub Pages.
Within Obsidian, my notes are divided between public and private directories. When I change something in the public directory and push it to the private repository, a GitHub Actions workflow rebuilds the Quartz site and deploys the generated files to the public repository using a deploy key. This allows me to update the website simply by editing and pushing my public notes from Obsidian, while keeping the rest of my vault private.
My main requirement was keeping my private and public notes separate while storing them in the same vault. This lets me move seamlessly between the two and update my website directly from Obsidian whenever I want.

topics/ai.title: ai
topics/ai.content:
AI in my workflow
Agentic AI goes beyond generating a single response. Given a goal, an agent can gather context, use tools, complete a sequence of actions, and verify the result while working within defined guardrails.
I use agentic AI for programming, scripting, automation, and my personal knowledge workflow. It helps me move from an idea to a working implementation by assisting with research, prototyping, troubleshooting, documentation, and validation.
Models I have used
I primarily use Codex, although I previously spent time with Claude and Gemini.





















ModelMy experienceClaudeClaude was highly capable, but it burned through its available tokens extremely quickly in my workflow. The quality was strong, but the usage limits made it difficult to rely on for sustained work.GeminiGemini was a good overall experience, but its programming performance did not consistently reach the level I wanted. Any advantages in price or speed mattered less when I needed more retries or intervention to reach the result I was aiming for.CodexCodex has been the best middle ground for me. For the projects I have worked on, it has felt as capable as Claude while giving me enough usage that I have not run into the same limits. I have not tested this comparison on particularly large or unusually complex projects, but it has been dependable for my current work.
I think about pricing and speed in terms of how much useful work I can complete, not only the subscription price or the time it takes to generate a response. A model that responds quickly can still slow down the overall task if it requires repeated corrections, while a capable model becomes less useful if its limits regularly interrupt the work. Codex currently gives me the best balance of capability, cost, speed, and available usage.
How my approach has changed
I initially tried to write as much of the code as I could myself, using AI mainly to answer questions, troubleshoot problems, and help refine what I had already written. Over time, I found that this was not always the most productive division of work.
I have recently become more comfortable handing most of the implementation to the agent. This lets me focus on the structure and design of the system: defining the goal, setting constraints, making architectural decisions, and checking that the pieces fit together. The agent can then handle much of the coding and the repetitive work involved in testing and refining it.
This does not mean giving up responsibility for the result. I treat the agent as a context-aware collaborator while remaining responsible for reviewing its work, testing the implementation, and deciding what is accepted or published.

topics/workflow.title: workflow
topics/workflow.content:
Personal knowledge workflow
My Obsidian vault is a working system for capturing ideas, connecting information, and maintaining context across projects. I rely on links, tags, search, and backlinks to make related knowledge discoverable without forcing everything into a deep folder hierarchy.
Capture and organization
New material begins as a quick capture. Useful ideas can then be refined into focused notes, connected to related subjects, and placed in the appropriate project or publishing context. Private material remains separate from content that is deliberately prepared for this website.
Context-aware agents
I use agentic AI as a collaborator within this system. Repository-level directives describe the vault’s structure and boundaries, while topic-specific context notes record the architecture, constraints, commands, and pitfalls associated with individual projects.
Before answering a question or making a change, an agent searches the vault, follows relevant links, and loads the context for the project it is working on. This grounds its work in my existing material instead of treating each request as an isolated conversation.
Changes and verification
Agents can help refine notes, update project context, modify site code, and run relevant checks. Each task follows the workflow appropriate to its scope. For example, changes to this website are built and reviewed locally on a staging branch before they can be published.
Human responsibility
The agent can gather context and carry out multi-step work, but it does not replace judgment. I remain responsible for reviewing results, testing code, protecting private information, and approving anything that becomes public.
